title: Where sounds come from, and what makes them loud or soft

summary.text: A closed bottle of rice sits on the table in silence. Shake it, and it rattles. Every sound comes from something moving: hands clapping, rain hitting a window, a crow calling, steam rushing out of a pressure cooker. The thing that makes a sound is called its sound source. Your child hunts for sound sources at home, tests which home-made shaker is loudest, and finds that a harder shake or a harder hit makes a louder sound.
summary.art: A girl shaking a plastic bottle half full of chana, with zigzag sound lines around it, and three more bottles lying still and silent on the table beside her.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Sit very still and listen for one whole minute. How many sounds can you hear? What is making each one?
intro.text: Even a quiet room is full of sounds: the fan, a bird outside, a scooter in the street, your own breathing. Every one of those sounds is made by something that is moving. In this unit you hunt for the things that make sounds. You also find out what makes a sound loud, and what makes it soft.
intro.art: A child sitting cross-legged on a mat with eyes closed, and small pictures floating around her: a ceiling fan, a crow at the window, a scooter and a ticking clock.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a sound source is: the thing that makes a sound.
By the end I can name sound sources at home and outside: people, other animals, things, and wind and rain.
By the end I can show that a sound comes from something moving, and that a still thing makes no sound.
By the end I can make the same thing sound loud or soft, by shaking or hitting it harder or more gently.
By the end I can find a sound source with my eyes closed, by listening carefully.

terms.meaning: A sound is anything we hear with our ears.
terms.example: A dog barking, a temple bell ringing and your friend's voice are all sounds.
terms.art: Three small pictures in a row: a dog barking, a brass bell ringing, and a girl talking, each with little sound lines.

terms.meaning: A sound source is the thing that makes a sound.
terms.example: When a pressure cooker whistles, the pressure cooker is the sound source.
terms.art: A pressure cooker on a stove with a puff of steam and a big whistle sound coming out of the top.

terms.meaning: To listen is to hear on purpose. You keep still and pay attention to the sounds.
terms.example: Close your eyes and listen. Can you hear the fan?
terms.art: A boy with eyes closed and one hand cupped behind his ear, and a ceiling fan above him.

terms.meaning: A loud sound is a big sound. You can hear it even from far away.
terms.example: Thunder, a bus horn and the drums at a temple festival are loud.
terms.art: A drummer beating a big drum with a stick, and large zigzag sound lines spreading out.

terms.meaning: A soft sound is a small, gentle sound. Soft sounds are also called quiet sounds.
terms.example: A whisper, a clock ticking and leaves rustling are soft.
terms.art: A girl whispering into her grandmother's ear, with one tiny sound line between them.

terms.meaning: Your voice is the sound you make when you talk, sing or shout. It starts in your throat, and your mouth shapes it.
terms.example: When you sing at Onam or say good morning, you are using your voice.
terms.art: A girl singing with her mouth open, a small arrow pointing to her throat.

explanations.definition: A sound source is the thing that makes a sound.
explanations.description: In the listening minute, every sound you heard came from somewhere. The whirr came from the fan. The caw came from a crow. The honk came from a scooter. Each of these is a sound source. Sometimes you can see the source, like a hand that claps. Sometimes it is hidden, like a neighbour's mixie behind a wall. Then you can find it by following the sound. As you walk towards the source, the sound gets louder.
examples: A crow cawing at the window
A neighbour's mixie behind the wall
Your own voice when you talk
explanations.art: A girl following a sound down a hallway towards a kitchen, the sound lines getting bigger as she gets closer to a mixie.

explanations.concept: A sound comes from something moving
explanations.definition: Every sound is made by something moving. When it stops moving, its sound stops.
explanations.description: In the Shaker Test, the bottles were silent while they sat on the table. When you shook them, the chana and the rice hit each other and the sides of the bottle, and you heard a rattle. Your hands make a clap only when they move and meet. Rain makes a sound when the drops hit the window. A crow calls by pushing air out from deep in the chest. Some moving is too small and too fast to see. Inside a phone, a tiny part moves back and forth very fast to make the sound you hear. In Class 3 you will learn the word for this fast shaking: vibrate.
examples: Chana hitting the inside of a bottle
A crow pushing air out to call
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a still bottle of chana on a table with no sound lines, and the same bottle being shaken with chana flying inside and sound lines around it.

explanations.definition: A loud sound is a big sound, and a soft sound is a small one. The harder something hits, shakes or blows, the louder its sound.
explanations.description: In the Shaker Test, a gentle shake made a soft rattle. A hard shake made a loud one. The same bottle can make a loud sound or a soft sound, depending on how hard you shake it. What hits matters too. Hard chana made a loud rattle. Soft cotton made almost no sound. And what it lands on matters. A spoon dropped on the bare floor goes clang. The same spoon dropped on a pillow makes almost no sound. A sound also gets softer as you move away from its source.
examples: Shaking the chana bottle hard, then gently
A spoon landing on the floor and on a pillow
A drum hit hard and hit softly
explanations.art: A girl shaking a bottle hard with big sound lines, next to a boy shaking the same kind of bottle gently with tiny sound lines.

explanations.definition: Sound sources can be people, other animals, things that people make, or nature itself.
explanations.description: People make sounds with their voices, their hands and their feet. Other animals make sounds too, in many ways. A crow and a cow call with their breath. A bee buzzes because her wings beat very fast. A cricket chirps by rubbing his wings together. Things that people make are sound sources too: a mixie, a bell, a bus, a pressure cooker. And nature makes sounds with no one helping: wind in the trees, rain on a roof, waves on a beach, thunder in a storm. Some sound sources are alive, and some are not.
examples: Waves on the beach at Puri
explanations.art: A page divided into four boxes: a family singing, a cow and a crow calling, a mixie and a bicycle bell, and rain and lightning over a sea.

explanations.concept: Why do so many birds sing in the early morning?
explanations.description: In many Indian cities, crows, mynas, bulbuls and koels are loudest around sunrise. Scientists call this the dawn chorus. They agree that birds sing to tell other birds who they are and where they live, and to find a mate. They still argue about why so much of the singing happens so early. Here are the main ideas.
examples: Bulbuls and mynas chattering in the morning

perspectives.explanation: Early morning is too dark to look for food well, so it is a good time to sing instead.
The air is often calm and still at dawn, so a song may carry further. Studies do not all agree that it does.
A bird who sings loudly first thing in the morning shows the neighbours that she or he is healthy and still there.

explanations.art: A row of birds on a balcony rail at sunrise, a crow, a myna, a bulbul and a koel, each with sound lines coming from the beak.

agreed.text: Every sound is made by something moving.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it. A bottle of rice sitting still makes no sound. Shake it, and it rattles at once.

agreed.text: A harder hit or a harder shake makes a louder sound.
agreed.evidence: In the Shaker Test, the same bottle of chana was loud when shaken hard and soft when shaken gently.

agreed.text: Many animals make sounds to call each other, including fish.
agreed.evidence: From the 1940s, the scientist Marie Poland Fish recorded the sounds of many kinds of fish and other sea animals, one kind at a time.

challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: Many sounds we notice are voices: people talking, dogs barking, birds calling.
challenging.against: Rain, wind, thunder and a falling spoon all make sounds, and none of them is alive. A sound comes from something moving, alive or not.

challenging.claim: Big things always make louder sounds than small things.
challenging.who: A common idea among children, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: An elephant's trumpet and a bus horn are big, loud sounds.
challenging.against: A tiny cricket can fill a room with chirping. A pillow is big, but dropping it makes almost no sound. And elephants walk very quietly, on soft, padded feet. How hard something moves, and what it hits, matter more than its size.

challenging.who: Many people, for a long time
challenging.for: We hear nothing when we look at fish in a tank or a pond.
challenging.against: Many fish make sounds underwater. Croaker fish drum with special muscles. Most of their sounds stay in the water, so people on land rarely hear them.

challenging.claim: A phone makes sound with nothing moving.
challenging.who: A common idea, because we cannot see anything move
challenging.for: A phone looks still when it plays music.
challenging.against: Inside the phone's speaker, a tiny part moves back and forth very fast. Put your finger lightly on a speaker while music plays, and you may feel it buzz.

big_questions.q: The shakers in the Shaker Test were silent while they sat on the table. Where was the rattle before you shook one?
big_questions.hint: Was the rattle waiting inside the bottle? Or did it begin when the chana started hitting the sides?

big_questions.q: Can anything move without making any sound at all?
big_questions.hint: Wave your hand very slowly through the air. Is there a sound too soft for you to hear? Some animals, like bats and dogs, can hear sounds that people cannot.

big_questions.q: When you talk, what part of you moves to make the sound?
big_questions.hint: Your breath comes up from your chest. Your throat, your tongue and your lips all move as you speak.

big_questions.q: A crow calls to other crows. What do you think she is telling them?
big_questions.hint: Crows call to warn each other about danger, like a cat nearby, and to keep in touch with their family. Listen to how a crow's call changes when a cat walks past.

big_questions.q: If you could hear every sound in the whole world at once, what would it be like?
big_questions.hint: Think of all the rain, the waves, the people talking and the animals calling, everywhere, all at the same time.

story.title: The Ting in the Night
story.note: Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Kavya, Arjun, Amma, Paati and Selvi are made up.
text: Kavya was six. She lived in a flat on the fourth floor in Madurai, with her Amma, her grandmother Paati, and her little brother Arjun, who was four.
One night the whole flat was dark and quiet. Amma was asleep. Paati was asleep. Even the fan was switched off, because the night was cool after the rain.
Then Kavya heard it. Ting.
She lay very still and listened. Ting. Ting.
Arjun sat up in his bed. "Akka," he whispered. Akka means big sister. "What is that? Is it a ghost?"
"I don't know yet," said Kavya. "But Paati always says that every sound comes from something. If we find what is moving, we find the sound."
Ting.

Kavya got out of bed and held Arjun's hand. They walked on tiptoe, so that their own feet would not make a sound. In the hall, the ting was a little louder. Near the kitchen door, it was louder still.
"It's in the kitchen," whispered Kavya. She switched on the small light.
The tap over the sink was dripping. A drop of water grew fat at the end of the tap. Then it fell. It landed in an empty steel bucket under the tap. Ting!
"There's your ghost," said Kavya. "A drop of water, falling on the steel."
Arjun laughed out loud. Then he put both hands over his mouth. "Shh! We'll wake Paati."
"Too late," said a voice. Paati was standing in the doorway, smiling. "Who is making a concert in my kitchen at midnight?"
"The tap!" said Arjun. "The drops hit the bucket. Ting, ting, ting."
Paati turned the tap as tight as it would go. The drops came more slowly, but they did not stop. Ting.
"This old tap needs mending," said Paati. "Selvi the plumber can come tomorrow. But how can we make it quiet tonight, so we can all sleep?"
Arjun thought hard. "Put a pillow in the bucket!"
"My pillow is not going in a bucket," said Paati.
Kavya looked around the kitchen. On the hook by the stove was a soft cotton towel. She folded it and laid it in the bottom of the bucket.
They waited. The drop grew fat. It fell. This time there was no ting. There was only a tiny pat, so soft they could hardly hear it.
"The drop still falls," said Kavya slowly. "But now it lands on something soft. So the sound is soft."
Paati nodded. "When something hits hard steel, you hear a loud ting. When it hits a soft towel, you hear only a little pat."
They all went back to bed. Kavya listened in the dark. She could not hear the tap at all now. She heard Arjun breathing, slow and sleepy. Far away, a dog barked once.

The next morning, Selvi the plumber came with her bag of tools. She opened the tap and put in a new rubber ring, called a washer. She closed it again. Arjun watched the end of the tap for a long time. No drop grew there. No drop fell.
"No more ting," said Arjun, a little sadly.
"No more moving water," said Kavya. "So no more sound."

That evening, Kavya drew a picture for her sound diary. She drew the tap, the drop, the steel bucket and the towel. Next to the steel bucket she drew big zigzag lines for a loud sound. Next to the towel she drew one tiny line for a soft sound.
Arjun looked at the picture. "Akka, can we find more sounds tomorrow?"
"Yes," said Kavya. "And for every one, we'll find what is moving."
story.epiphany: Every sound comes from something moving. The falling drop made a loud ting on hard steel and only a soft pat on a soft towel. When the tap was mended and no drop fell, the sound stopped.
ask: What was making the ting in the night?
How did Kavya find where the sound was coming from?
Why did the drop make only a soft pat when it fell on the towel?
After Selvi mended the tap, the ting stopped for good. Why?
art: A dark bedroom in a flat at night, a girl and a small boy sitting up in their beds, listening, with a small 'ting' drawn in the air.
The girl and the boy tiptoeing hand in hand down a dark hallway towards a kitchen door.
A dripping kitchen tap and a drop falling into an empty steel bucket, with a bright 'ting' and sound lines.
A grandmother in the kitchen doorway smiling, while the girl lays a folded towel in the bucket.
A woman plumber with a bag of tools fixing the tap, and the boy watching closely.

experiments.title: The Shaker Test: which shaker is loudest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make four shakers that look the same, with something different inside each one. You guess which will be loudest. Then you shake them and listen.
experiments.question: Does what is inside a shaker change how loud it sounds? And does shaking harder make it louder?
experiments.predict: Look at the four shakers: chana, rice, cotton and nothing. Which will be loudest? Which will be softest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four shakers are the same kind of bottle or box. Chana and rice are two big spoons each. The cotton is two balls, which fill about the same space. The empty one has nothing in it. Only what is inside is different. We shake each one five times, the same way.
results_table: My guess: loud, middle or soft?
What I heard: loud, middle or soft?

materials.item: 4 small plastic bottles with caps, all the same, or 4 small plastic or steel boxes with tight lids
2 big spoons of dry chana, or any big dry bean like rajma
2 big spoons of uncooked rice
2 balls of cotton wool, or a small rolled-up piece of old cloth
a big spoon, and a sheet of paper rolled into a funnel
4 small pieces of paper, a pencil and tape, for picture labels
a dupatta or a towel, to hide the shakers

experiments.safety: Chana and rice are small. Watch younger children so they do not put them in their mouth, nose or ears. Close the caps tightly.

schedule.what: Make four shakers, guess which will be loudest, then shake them and listen.

experiments.record: Draw the four shakers in a line, from the loudest to the softest. Draw big zigzag lines around the loudest one, and tiny lines, or none, around the softest.

setup.art: Four empty plastic bottles in a row, with small bowls of chana, rice and cotton balls beside them, and a paper funnel.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bottles. Leave one empty. Close the caps.

setup.art: Four closed bottles standing still on a table, each with a picture label, and a girl leaning in to listen.
setup.caption: 2. Listen to the shakers sitting still.

setup.art: A girl with her eyes closed while a grown-up shakes a bottle under a dupatta.
setup.caption: 3. Shake each one five times. Listen with your eyes closed.

setup.art: The girl shaking the chana bottle gently with small sound lines, then hard with big sound lines.
setup.caption: 4. Shake the chana bottle gently, then hard.

flow.do: 1. Put two big spoons of chana in the first bottle, through the paper funnel. 2. Put two big spoons of rice in the second. 3. Push two cotton balls into the third. 4. Leave the fourth empty. 5. Close all the caps tightly.
flow.say: We are making four shakers. Each one gets something different inside. Let's draw a picture label for each one.
flow.kid: Help fill the bottles. Close the caps tight. Draw a picture label for each.
flow.parent: Picture labels help a child who cannot read yet: a bean, a grain of rice, a cloud of cotton and an empty circle.

flow.do: Put all four shakers on the table. Ask your child to sit very still, lean close and listen for ten seconds.
flow.say: Our shakers are sitting on the table. Put your ear close and listen very carefully. Can you hear them?
flow.kid: Put your ear close to the shakers. Can you hear them?

good: They make no sound when they sit still.

flow.parent: The still shakers are silent. Let your child notice this, and come back to it at the end. Don't explain it yet.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put the shakers in a line, from 'will be loudest' to 'will be softest'. 2. Draw or write the guesses in the table. A grown-up writes for a child who cannot write yet.
flow.say: Soon you will shake each one. Which will be loudest? Put it at this end. Which will be softest? Put it at the other end. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which shaker will be loudest? Which will be softest? Line them up. Why?

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: The chana is big and hard.
The rice has lots and lots of grains.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children think the rice will be loudest, because there are so many grains. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes each shaker five times, the same way. 2. Hide all four under the dupatta. 3. Your child closes their eyes. 4. Shake one at a time under the dupatta. 5. Each time, your child says loud, middle or soft.
flow.say: Shake each one five times. Now close your eyes. I will shake one under the dupatta. Is it loud, middle or soft? Which one do you think it is?
flow.kid: Shake each one five times. Now close your eyes. Is it loud, middle or soft?

good: The empty one made almost no sound.

flow.parent: Usually the chana is loudest, and the rice makes a softer, hissing rattle. The cotton and the empty bottle are nearly silent. If two sound alike, shake them one after the other, again. Write what your child heard in the table.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the chana shaker. 2. Ask them to shake it very gently. 3. Then very hard. 4. Then very gently again.
flow.say: Now shake the chana one very gently. Now shake it hard. Now gently again. What changes?
flow.kid: Shake it gently. Now shake it hard. What changes?

good: A hard shake made a big sound.

check.q: How do you make the chana shaker louder?
check.why: A harder shake makes the chana hit the bottle harder, so the sound is louder. A gentle shake makes a soft sound, and a still shaker makes no sound at all.

flow.do: 1. Open the chana shaker and the cotton shaker. 2. Give your child one chana and one cotton ball. 3. Ask them to tap each one on the table.
flow.say: Tap the chana on the table. Now tap the cotton. Which one makes a sound?
flow.kid: Tap a chana on the table. Now tap the cotton. Which makes a sound?

good: The cotton is soft, so it makes almost no sound.

flow.parent: This shows why the cotton shaker was so quiet. Hard things hitting make loud sounds. Soft things hitting make soft sounds.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell you three things. Write them down in your child's words. Ask what the shakers did while they sat still.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you hear? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you think. Say what you heard. Say why.
flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this. 'The shakers were silent when they sat still. The chana was loudest. Shaking hard made it louder. Hard chana makes a loud sound, and soft cotton makes a soft sound.'

experiments.title: Soft Landing: what makes a falling spoon quiet?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop a steel spoon onto different things and listen. Does the sound change with what the spoon lands on?
experiments.question: When a steel spoon falls, does what it lands on change how loud the sound is?
experiments.predict: We will drop a spoon onto the bare floor, a folded newspaper, a folded towel and a pillow. Which will be loudest? Which will be softest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same spoon every time. We drop it from the same height, your knee. We let it fall, and never throw it. At the end we change the height on purpose, to see what it does.
results_table: What I heard: loud or soft?

materials.item: a steel spoon
a newspaper, folded into four
a towel, folded into four
a pillow or a cushion
a patch of floor with no rug

schedule.what: Drop a spoon onto four different things and listen to each landing.

experiments.record: Draw the four landing places in a row. Draw big zigzag lines next to the loudest landing, and one tiny line next to the softest.

setup.art: A bare tiled floor with a folded newspaper, a folded towel and a pillow laid in a row, and a steel spoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the newspaper, the towel and the pillow on the floor.

setup.art: A boy holding a steel spoon at knee height above the bare floor, about to let go.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the spoon at your knee. Let it fall.

setup.art: The spoon landing on a pillow with no sound lines, next to the spoon landing on the bare floor with big sound lines.
setup.caption: 3. Listen to each landing. Which is loud? Which is soft?

flow.do: Lay the folded newspaper, the folded towel and the pillow on the floor in a row. Leave a patch of bare floor next to them.
flow.say: Here are four landing places for our spoon: the bare floor, the newspaper, the towel and the pillow.
flow.kid: Look at the four landing places. Touch each one.

flow.do: Ask your child to point to the landing that will be loudest, and the one that will be softest. Write or draw the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Which landing will make the loudest sound? Which will make the softest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which will be loudest? Which will be softest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the pillow will be soft?
good: It is soft, so the spoon will not bang.

flow.parent: Don't say what will happen. Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the spoon at knee height over each landing place. 2. They let it fall, without throwing. 3. Drop it twice on each one. 4. Your child says loud or soft each time.
flow.say: Hold the spoon at your knee. Let it go. Listen. Was it loud or soft? Let's try it twice on each place.
flow.kid: Hold the spoon at your knee. Let it go. Loud or soft?

good: It went clang on the floor.
On the pillow I could hardly hear it.

flow.parent: The bare floor is loudest. The newspaper is a little softer, the towel is softer still, and the pillow is nearly silent.

flow.do: 1. Your child drops the spoon on the bare floor from knee height. 2. Then from as high as their shoulder.
flow.say: Now drop it on the floor from your knee. Now from your shoulder. Which was louder?
flow.kid: Drop it from your knee. Now drop it from your shoulder. Which was louder?

good: The higher drop hit the floor harder.

check.q: The spoon was dropped from a knee and from a shoulder. Which drop was louder?
check.why: From higher up, the spoon falls faster and hits the floor harder. A harder hit makes a louder sound.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell you three things. Write them down in your child's words.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you hear? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you think. Say what you heard. Say why.
flow.parent: A strong answer: 'The floor was loudest and the pillow was softest. The spoon hits the hard floor hard. The soft pillow catches it gently.'

activities.title: One Minute of Listening
activities.context: In this activity you sit still for one minute and listen. Then you name the sound source of every sound you heard, and draw a sound map.

materials.item: nothing to buy: a place to sit quietly
a sheet of paper and crayons

schedule.what: Listen for one minute, name each sound source, then draw a sound map.

activities.record: A sound map: draw yourself in the middle of the page. Around you, draw every sound source you heard. Draw loud ones big and soft ones small.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child sitting on a mat with their eyes closed, the child holding up three fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Close your eyes. Count the sounds on your fingers.

setup.art: A child's drawing with a stick figure in the middle and a fan, a crow, a scooter and a clock drawn around the figure, big and small.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a sound map of what you heard.

flow.do: 1. Sit with your child somewhere in the home. 2. Both close your eyes. 3. Stay silent for one minute. 4. Your child counts each new sound on their fingers.
flow.say: Let's close our eyes and be very still for one minute. Each time you hear a new sound, put up one finger.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Keep still. Put up a finger for each sound.

flow.do: Ask your child to name each sound, and what made it. Write a short list.
flow.say: How many sounds did you hear? Tell me each one. What made that sound? Was it a person, an animal, a thing, or the wind or rain?
flow.kid: Tell me each sound. What made it?

ask.q: Were there more sounds than you thought?
good: I heard sounds I never noticed.

flow.parent: Good answers in an Indian home: the fan, a pressure cooker, a scooter horn, a crow, a vegetable seller calling, a neighbour's TV, the fridge, our own breathing.

flow.do: Give your child paper and crayons. They draw themselves in the middle, and each sound source around them.
flow.say: Draw yourself in the middle. Now draw each thing that made a sound. Make the loud ones big and the soft ones small.
flow.kid: Draw yourself in the middle. Draw each sound around you. Loud ones big, soft ones small.

activities.title: My Body Band
activities.context: In this activity you make sounds with your own body, each one loud and then soft. Your body is a sound source too.

materials.item: nothing to buy: just your body

schedule.what: Make sounds with hands, feet, mouth and voice, loud and soft, then play a pattern.

activities.record: Draw the body part that made your favourite sound, with sound lines around it.

setup.art: A girl clapping, a boy stamping, and a parent patting their knees, all in a circle on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Make sounds with your hands, feet and mouth.

setup.art: The girl clapping hard with big sound lines, and then clapping with two fingers with tiny sound lines.
setup.caption: 2. Make each sound loud, then soft.

flow.do: Make these sounds together, one at a time: clap, stamp, pat your knees, click your tongue, hum. After each one, ask what moved.
flow.say: Let's make sounds with our bodies. Clap. Stamp. Pat your knees. Click your tongue. Hum. What moved each time?
flow.kid: Clap. Stamp. Pat your knees. Click your tongue. Hum. What moved?

flow.do: Make each sound loud, then soft. For a soft clap, clap with two fingers on your palm.
flow.say: Now make each sound loud. Now make it soft. How did you make it soft?
flow.kid: Make each sound loud. Now make it soft. How did you do it?

ask.q: How did you make the clap soft?

flow.parent: Look for the idea that a gentle movement makes a soft sound and a hard movement makes a loud one.

flow.do: Play a pattern and ask your child to copy it. Then let them make one for you. Try: clap, clap, stamp. Then soft clap, soft clap, loud stamp.
flow.say: Copy me. Clap, clap, stamp. Now soft clap, soft clap, loud stamp. Now you make one for me to copy.
flow.kid: Copy the pattern. Now make your own for me to copy.

activities.title: Who Is Calling? Listening at the window
activities.context: In this activity you listen at a window for the voices of other animals, and find out who is calling.

materials.item: nothing to buy: a window or a balcony
paper and crayons

schedule.what: Listen at the window for animal calls, copy them softly, and draw the callers.

activities.record: Draw each animal you heard, with their call written next to them by a grown-up.

setup.art: A boy and a parent at an open window of a flat, listening, with a crow on a nearby wire and pigeons on a ledge.
setup.caption: 1. Listen at the window. Who is calling?

setup.art: The boy drawing a crow and a pigeon, with 'caw' and 'coo' written beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the callers you heard.

flow.do: Stand at a window or a balcony with your child. Listen quietly together for animal sounds. Early morning or evening is best.
flow.say: Let's listen for animals. Who can you hear? Can you see who is calling?
flow.kid: Listen for animals. Who is calling? Can you see them?
flow.parent: Crows, pigeons, mynas, dogs and cats live in almost every Indian city. If you hear no animals today, listen for people and traffic instead, and try again early tomorrow morning.

flow.do: Copy each call softly together. Ask how the animal makes that sound.
flow.say: Let's copy the crow, softly. Caw. How does a crow make that sound?
flow.kid: Copy the call softly. How does the animal make that sound?

flow.do: Your child draws the callers. You write each call beside its animal.
flow.say: Draw each animal you heard. I will write their call next to them.
flow.kid: Draw each animal you heard.

activities.title: Sound Scavenger Hunt
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for ten sound sources: five from nature and five made by people.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded in half, and a pencil

schedule.what: Find five sound sources from nature and five made by people.

activities.record: On one half of the paper, draw five sound sources from nature. On the other half, draw five made by people.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded in half, with a leaf drawn at the top of one side and a bell at the top of the other.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the paper. One side for nature, one side for things people made.

setup.art: A girl at a balcony pointing at rain falling, with a mixie and a bicycle visible inside and outside.
setup.caption: 2. Hunt for sounds and draw each one on the right side.

flow.do: Fold the paper in half. Draw a leaf at the top of one half, for nature. Draw a bell at the top of the other, for things people made.
flow.say: We are going to hunt for ten sound sources. Five from nature, like rain or a bird. Five made by people, like a bell or a mixie.
flow.kid: Find five sounds from nature. Find five sounds people made.

flow.do: Walk around the home and look out of the windows. For each sound your child finds, they draw it on the right half.
flow.say: What can you hear? What is making it? Is it from nature, or did people make it?
flow.kid: Listen. What is making that sound? Nature or people?

ask.q: Is the wind from nature or made by people?

flow.parent: Nature: wind, rain, birds, dogs, insects, a person's own voice and breathing. Made by people: fan, mixie, fridge, doorbell, scooter, TV. Let your child decide where people's own voices go, and ask why.

flow.do: Count each half together.
flow.say: How many from nature? How many made by people? Which side has more?
flow.kid: Count each side. Which has more?

games.title: Sound Detective: what made that sound?
games.players: 2 or more: a sound maker and a detective. With 2 players, the grown-up and the child take turns at both.
games.context: This is a listening game. The detective closes their eyes, the sound maker makes a sound, and the detective says what made it and what moved.

items.b: Keys. The keys hit each other.

items.f: Pour water from a jug into a steel tumbler.
items.b: Water. The water splashes into the tumbler.
Hands. Your hands hit each other.
A door. The door hits its frame.

items.f: Tap a pencil on a table.
items.b: A pencil. The pencil hits the table.

items.f: Open and close a zip on a bag.
items.b: A zip. Its little teeth click together.
Hands. Your hands rub against each other.
A plastic bag. It crinkles as it folds.

items.f: Blow out a long breath: whoosh.
items.b: Breath. Air rushes out of your mouth.

items.f: Drop a coin on the floor.
items.b: A coin. It hits the floor and bounces.

items.f: Shake a closed bottle with chana inside.
items.b: A bottle of chana. The chana hits the inside of the bottle.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, front side down. Choose a detective and a sound maker.
The sound maker turns over the top card and reads the front quietly. If the sound maker cannot read yet, the grown-up whispers it to them.
Then the detective sits with their back turned and eyes closed.
The sound maker makes that sound, two times.
The detective says what made the sound, and what moved.
The detective turns round. The sound maker shows the back of the card. If the detective was right, they keep the card. If not, the card goes to the side.

With 2 players, swap roles after six cards. With 3 or more, everyone else is a detective, the first to say the right answer keeps the card, and the sound maker's turn passes to the next person after each card.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most cards is the best detective. If it is a tie, you are all best detectives.

setup.art: A girl sitting with her back turned and eyes closed, and a parent behind her shaking a bunch of keys.
setup.caption: 1. The detective closes their eyes. The sound maker makes a sound.

setup.art: The girl turned round, pointing at the keys and smiling, holding a card.
setup.caption: 2. The detective says what made it, then turns to look.

flow.do: Read the rules together. Decide who is the first detective. Collect what the cards need. You need keys, newspaper, a jug of water and a steel tumbler. You also need a pencil, a bag with a zip, a plastic bag, a coin and a closed bottle with chana inside.
flow.say: You are the detective. Close your eyes and listen. You have to tell me what made the sound, and what moved.
flow.kid: You are the detective. Close your eyes. What made the sound?

flow.do: Play six cards with your child as detective. After each guess, ask what moved, then let them turn and look.
flow.say: Listen. What made that sound? What moved? Turn round and see if you were right.
flow.kid: Listen. What made that sound? What moved? Now turn and look.

ask.q: What moved to make the keys jingle?

flow.parent: The tricky cards are the breath, the rubbing hands and the plastic bag. If your child is stuck, make the sound once more, a little louder.

flow.do: Swap roles for the last six cards. Whisper each card to your child, then close your eyes and guess.
flow.say: Now you are the sound maker. I will whisper the card to you. Make the sound, and I will guess.
flow.kid: Now you make the sounds. Can you trick me?

check.q: In every sound in this game, what was always happening?
check.why: Every sound came from something moving: keys hitting, paper tearing, water splashing, hands clapping. When nothing moves, there is no sound.

games.title: Stamp, Tiptoe, Freeze
games.players: 1 or more players, and a grown-up as the drummer.
games.context: This is a moving game. The drummer beats loudly or softly on an upside-down bucket. Players stamp for loud, tiptoe for soft, and freeze when the sound stops.
rules: The drummer turns a plastic bucket or a big steel vessel upside down, and beats it with a wooden spoon.
The drummer takes a card and plays what it says.
Loud beats: players stamp around with big, heavy steps.
Soft beats: players tiptoe, quiet as a cat.
No sound: players freeze like statues until the next beat.
Anyone who moves in the silence swaps places with the drummer, and the new drummer plays the cards that are left. With one player, the player and the grown-up swap.
The game ends when all eight cards are played. Shuffle them and play again if you like.

setup.art: A parent beating an upside-down blue plastic bucket with a wooden spoon, and two children stamping with big steps.
setup.caption: 1. Loud beats: stamp. Soft beats: tiptoe.

setup.art: The two children frozen like statues with arms in the air, and the spoon held still above the bucket.
setup.caption: 2. No sound: freeze!

flow.do: Turn the bucket upside down. Show one loud beat and one soft beat.
flow.say: This is a loud beat. This is a soft beat. When it is loud, stamp. When it is soft, tiptoe. When it stops, freeze.
flow.kid: Loud: stamp. Soft: tiptoe. No sound: freeze.

flow.do: Play through the eight drummer cards. Then shuffle them and play again if there is time.
flow.say: Listen. Is it loud or soft? Now it has stopped. Freeze!
flow.kid: Listen. Loud or soft? Silence: freeze!
flow.parent: Watch whether your child changes their steps as soon as the sound changes. That shows careful listening.

flow.do: Let your child be the drummer. Ask how they make a beat loud or soft.
flow.say: Now you are the drummer. How will you make a loud beat? How will you make a soft one?
flow.kid: You are the drummer now. Make loud beats and soft beats.

ask.q: How do you make a loud beat?
good: Bang it with a big swing.

ask.q: How do you make a soft beat?

projects.title: My Loud and Soft Sound Book
projects.context: In this project you make a small book of sound sources. Each page has a loud sound on one side and a soft sound on the other.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or stitched into a book
crayons or sketch pens

schedule.what: Make the book and draw two pages: one loud sound source and one soft sound source on each.
Find more sounds and finish the book, then read it to someone and make each sound.

setup.art: Three folded sheets of paper being stapled into a small book, with crayons beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and staple the paper into a book.

setup.art: An open page with a big bus horn drawn on the left under the word LOUD and a small ticking clock on the right under SOFT.
setup.caption: 2. On each page, draw a loud sound and a soft sound.

flow.do: A grown-up folds the sheets and staples them into a book. Write LOUD at the top of each left page and SOFT at the top of each right page.
flow.say: We are making a sound book. Each left page is for a loud sound. Each right page is for a soft sound.
flow.kid: Left page: a loud sound. Right page: a soft sound.

flow.do: Your child draws a loud sound source and a soft sound source on the first two pages. Write the names for them.
flow.say: Think of a loud sound in our home. Draw what makes it. Now a soft sound. What makes it?
flow.kid: Draw a loud sound source. Now draw a soft one.

ask.q: What makes your loud sound loud?

flow.do: On day 2, your child fills the other pages, then reads the book to a family member. For each page, they make the sound, loud or soft.
flow.say: Let's finish the book. Then read it to someone at home, and make each sound as you show them the page.
flow.kid: Finish your book. Read it to someone. Make each sound.
flow.parent: Some sounds can be made both loud and soft, like a clap or a drum. If your child notices this, ask how they would draw it.

challenges.title: Don't Wake the Baby
challenges.context: This is a problem to solve. Pretend a baby is sleeping. Can you put away steel vessels without a loud clang?
challenges.problem: Pretend a baby is asleep in the next room. You must carry three steel tumblers and a steel plate to the kitchen and put them on the shelf. How can you do it so quietly that the baby does not wake up?
constraints: Everything must end up on the kitchen shelf.
Use only things you already have at home.
Pretend the baby wakes at any loud clang.
materials: a hand towel or a napkin
general: Carry one thing at a time.
Put each thing down slowly and gently.
creative: Lay a folded towel on the tray, so the tumblers stand on something soft.
Put a napkin between the tumblers so they do not touch.
Slide each tumbler onto the shelf instead of setting it down from above.
challenges.your_turn: Try it with a grown-up listening with eyes closed. Did they hear a clang? Which idea made the softest sound? Why?

setup.art: A girl holding three steel tumblers and a steel plate, with a cradle in the next room.
setup.caption: 1. The baby is asleep. How can you carry these without a clang?

setup.art: The girl carrying the tumblers on a tray covered with a folded towel, walking on tiptoe.
setup.caption: 2. Try your ideas. Which is quietest?

flow.do: Read the problem. Put the tumblers and the plate on the floor in one room, and the tray and towel beside them.
flow.say: A baby is sleeping in the next room. You must carry these to the kitchen shelf. How can you do it without a clang?
flow.kid: A baby is sleeping. Carry these without a clang. How will you do it?

flow.do: Let your child try their ideas. You sit with your eyes closed and listen. Say 'clang' if you hear a loud sound.
flow.say: Try your idea. I will close my eyes and listen. If I hear a clang, the pretend baby wakes up.
flow.kid: Try your idea. Don't let me hear a clang!
flow.parent: Help only if asked. Good ideas use something soft between the steel things, or slow, gentle movements.

flow.do: Ask your child which way was quietest, and why.
flow.say: Which way was quietest? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which way was quietest? Why?

good: Steel landing on a soft towel makes a soft sound.

items.p: A grown-up reads each sound. Who or what made it? Draw a line to the right group: people, other animals, or things.
items.why: Every sound has a source. People make sounds with their voices. Other animals call, buzz and moo. Things that people make, like bells and mixies, make sounds when they move.
items.art: Six small pictures: a crying baby, a cow, a doorbell, a woman singing, a bee and a mixie, with three boxes labelled with a face, a paw and a gear.

items.p: Three of these are making a sound right now. Which one is silent? Circle it.
opts: A spoon lying still on a table
items.why: The spoon is lying still, so it makes no sound. The bell, the dog and the hands are all moving, so we hear them.
items.art: Four pictures in a row: a swinging bell, a barking dog, a spoon on a table and two clapping hands.

items.p: A grown-up reads the words. Draw a line from each sound to its source.
items.why: Each sound tells us its source. A crow caws, a pressure cooker whistles when steam rushes out, a cow moos and a bicycle bell rings when you press it.
items.art: Four sound words on the left. On the right, a crow, a pressure cooker, a cow and a bicycle bell.

items.p: In the Shaker Test, a child shook the chana shaker gently, then hard. When was it louder?
items.why: A hard shake makes the chana hit the bottle harder, so the sound is louder. A gentle shake makes a soft sound.

items.p: Draw one thing in your home that makes a loud sound. Then draw one thing that makes a soft sound.
items.a: One loud sound source, such as a pressure cooker, a mixie or a doorbell, and one soft sound source, such as a clock, a fan or a whisper.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real sound source for each, and draws something that moves to make the sound.
items.art: Two empty boxes, one with big zigzag lines in the corner and one with a single tiny line.

items.p: Your own body can be a sound source when you clap or stamp.
items.why: True. When you clap, your hands move and meet. When you stamp, your foot hits the floor. Anything that moves can make a sound, and your body moves.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. When the shaker rattled, what was moving?
items.a: The chana, or the rice, was moving inside the bottle. It hit the other grains and the sides of the bottle.
items.why: A strong answer names what moved inside the shaker, and says that it hit something.

items.p: Look at the kitchen. A grown-up points to each thing. Say 'loud', 'soft' or 'silent', and the grown-up writes it.
labels: a steel spoon lying on the shelf
items.why: The pressure cooker and the mixie make loud sounds. A drip makes a soft sound. The spoon is not moving, so it is silent.
items.art: A kitchen with a pressure cooker letting out steam, a mixie running, a tap dripping into a sink and a spoon on a shelf, each with an empty label.

items.p: Look at the street picture. Count the sound sources that are making a sound. Write the number.
items.why: There are 5 sound sources making sounds: an auto honking, a vegetable seller calling, a dog barking, a crow cawing and a temple bell ringing. The parked bicycle is not making a sound, because nothing is moving it.
items.art: A busy Indian street with an auto honking, a woman with a vegetable cart calling out, a barking dog, a crow on a wire, a temple bell being rung, and a parked bicycle.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 1, wants to call her friend from across the playground. Three children have ideas.

views.says: Shout her name. A loud shout goes far.
Clap your hands hard. It is loud, and you won't hurt your throat.
Walk over and talk softly. Then nobody else is disturbed.

items.ask: Which idea would you choose? Why? Then say one good thing about someone else's idea.
items.a: Any choice with a good reason. A shout is loud and goes far but can disturb others. A clap is loud and saves your voice, but your friend may not know it is for her. Walking over is quiet and clear but takes longer.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason, and fairly says what is good about another idea. Each idea makes a different sound source loud or soft.

items.p: A grown-up reads these steps of the Shaker Test. Number them 1, 2 and 3 in the right order.
items: Line up the shakers from loud to soft
Guess which shaker will be loudest
Shake each shaker five times and listen
a: Guess which shaker will be loudest
Shake each shaker five times and listen
Line up the shakers from loud to soft
items.why: First we guess, then we test by shaking and listening, then we line them up by what we heard.

items.p: Meera, a girl in Class 1, rings a bell on the table. Then she walks to the other side of the room and listens. How does the ring sound from far away?
items.why: A sound gets softer as you move away from its source. That is why you can find a hidden sound by walking towards where it gets louder.

items.p: A phone is playing a song. Where is the sound coming from?
opts: A tiny part inside the phone that moves very fast
The air in the room, all by itself
items.why: Inside the phone's speaker, a tiny part moves back and forth very fast. That moving part is the sound source. We cannot see it move, but it is moving.

items.p: Only living things can make sounds.
items.why: False. Rain, wind, thunder and a falling spoon all make sounds, and none of them is alive. Anything that moves can make a sound.

items.p: A thing that makes a sound is called a sound ___. A grown-up can help write the word.
items.why: A sound source is the thing that makes a sound, like a bell, a crow or your own voice.

items.p: A grown-up reads the words. Each of these animals makes a sound in a different way. Draw a line to show how.
items.why: Animals make sounds in many ways. A bee's buzz comes from her fast-beating wings. A male cricket rubs his wings together to chirp. A crow pushes air out to call. A woodpecker hammers on wood with a beak.
items.art: A bee, a cricket, a crow and a woodpecker on the left. On the right, small pictures of beating wings, rubbing wings, an open beak and a beak tapping a tree.

items.p: Your friend says big things are always louder than small things. A cricket is tiny, and a pillow is big. Is your friend right? Say why, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: No. A tiny cricket can chirp loudly enough to fill a room. A big pillow makes almost no sound when it falls. How hard something moves, and what it hits, matter more than its size.
items.why: A strong answer uses an example of a small, loud thing or a big, quiet thing to show the idea is wrong.

items.p: Draw yourself tapping a steel dabba twice: once to make a soft sound and once to make a loud sound. Show how your hand moves each time.
items.a: Two drawings. For the soft sound, a small, gentle movement and small sound lines. For the loud sound, a big swing and big sound lines.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that a bigger, harder movement makes a louder sound.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, each with a small steel dabba drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Meera, a girl aged 8, watches rain fall on a window with her mother and her grandfather. They disagree about the sound source.

views.says: The raindrops are the sound source. They are what is falling.
The window is the sound source. The glass shakes when the drops hit it.
Both of them. The drops hit, and the glass moves.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say something true about another person's idea.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both the drops and the glass move when a drop hits. Rain sounds different on a window, a tin roof and a leaf, so what the drops land on matters too.
items.why: A sound often comes from two things meeting. The drop moves, and the glass it hits moves too. A strong answer gives a reason and fairly says what is right about another view.

items.p: Guess before you try. Would a shaker full of coins be louder or softer than a shaker full of cotton? Why? Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Louder. Coins are hard and heavy, so they hit the bottle hard. Cotton is soft, so it hits gently and makes almost no sound.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the Shaker Test showed: hard things hitting make loud sounds and soft things make soft sounds.

opts: The ear that hears a sound
The thing that makes a sound
quiz.why: A sound source is the thing that makes a sound, like a bell or a crow. The ear hears the sound, but it does not make it.

quiz.p: A pressure cooker whistles in the kitchen. What is the sound source?
quiz.why: The sound comes from the pressure cooker, as steam rushes out of the top.

quiz.p: Which of these sound sources is not alive?
quiz.why: Rain is not alive, but it still makes a sound when the drops hit the roof. The crow and the cow are living beings who call with their breath.

quiz.p: A temple bell hangs still. Nobody touches it. What do you hear from the bell?
quiz.why: A still bell makes no sound. It rings only when something moves it, like a hand pulling the rope.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 1, claps his hands. What moved to make the sound?
quiz.why: His hands moved and hit each other. That is what made the clap.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 1, wants a louder sound from her drum. What should she do?
quiz.why: A harder hit makes a louder sound. A gentle hit makes a soft sound, and no hit makes no sound.

quiz.p: Remember the Shaker Test, with chana, rice, cotton and an empty bottle. Which shaker with something inside made the softest sound?
quiz.why: Cotton is soft, so it hits the bottle gently and makes almost no sound. Hard chana makes the loudest rattle.

quiz.p: Why is a whisper a soft sound?
opts: Only a little air moves, gently
quiz.why: When you whisper, only a little air moves out of your mouth, gently. A shout pushes out much more air, much harder.

quiz.p: Your eyes are closed. You hear keys jingling. What is moving?
quiz.why: Every sound comes from something moving. Jingling keys are moving and hitting each other.

quiz.p: Sneha, a girl in Class 1, hears a sound behind a door, but she cannot see what made it. How can she find the sound source?
opts: Walk towards where the sound gets louder
quiz.why: A sound gets louder as you get closer to its source. Following the sound leads you to it, as the children did in the story.

videos.title: A cricket chirping, close up
videos.why: Shows a tiny sound source making a loud sound, by rubbing the wings together.
videos.check: Find real close-up footage of a male field cricket chirping, from a nature channel or a university. Check that the wings are seen rubbing while the sound plays, and that it is not animation.

videos.title: Fish sounds recorded underwater
videos.why: Lets children hear sound sources most people never hear: croakers, toadfish and snapping shrimp.
videos.check: Find a short recording from a real research group or aquarium that names each animal as their sound plays. Check the animals named are correct.

videos.title: Birds singing at dawn in an Indian city
videos.why: A real dawn chorus to listen to with eyes closed, and to pick out the different callers.
videos.check: Find a real recording of morning birdsong in an Indian city or park, ideally naming the birds, such as from a bird-watching group. Check that it is not mixed with music.

applications: Horns on buses, autos and scooters, and bells on bicycles, warn people to move out of the way.
A pressure cooker whistles when steam rushes out. The whistles tell the cook how the cooking is going.
Doctors listen to your heart with a stethoscope. Each heartbeat makes a sound as the little doors inside the heart, called valves, close.
School bells, fire alarms and ambulance sirens are made loud on purpose, so that everyone hears them.
Scientists put microphones in the sea to listen to fish, whales and dolphins, and to learn how they are living.

spotted.text: At Thrissur Pooram in Kerala, long rows of drummers play the chenda together, and the sound fills the town.
spotted.art: Rows of drummers in white mundus playing tall chenda drums in front of decorated elephants.

spotted.text: During Durga Puja in Kolkata, drummers play the dhak, a big drum hung from the shoulder.
spotted.art: A drummer with a big dhak hanging from his shoulder, with a bunch of white feathers on top, in front of a lit pandal.

spotted.text: In summer, the koel calls 'koo-ooo' loudly from trees in cities across India. The loud caller is the male, a black bird with red eyes.
spotted.art: A glossy black koel with red eyes sitting in a mango tree, beak open in a call.

spotted.text: At Bohag Bihu in Assam, people play the dhol and blow the pepa, a pipe made from a buffalo horn.
spotted.art: Young people dancing in a field, one beating a dhol and one blowing a curved pepa.

spotted.text: In many homes, a bell rings in the morning puja, and a pressure cooker whistles while lunch is cooking.
spotted.art: A kitchen with a small brass bell on a shelf and a pressure cooker whistling on the stove.

open_questions.q: What are crows saying to each other?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know crows have many different calls, for danger, for food and for their family. Nobody yet understands everything the calls mean.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of fish make sounds?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep finding fish who make sounds, and many kinds of fish have never been listened to carefully.

open_questions.q: Why do so many birds sing most at dawn?
open_questions.why_open: There are several good ideas, such as calm morning air or too little light to find food. Scientists are still testing which ones are right.

ask_kids: What is the loudest sound you heard today? What made it?
What is the softest sound in this room right now?
Can you make a sound with your elbow? With your nose?
Which animal near our home is the loudest caller?
How could you make a spoon make a sound? A loud one? A soft one?
When everyone is asleep at night, what sounds can you still hear?

jokes.j: Why was the shaker so cheerful?
What is a cricket's favourite game?
Why did the crow sit on the phone wire?
What did one hand say to the other hand?
jokes.a: Let's get together and make some noise!

jokes.j: What did the pillow say to the falling spoon?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I'll catch you softly!

jokes.j: What do you call a whisper that grew up?
Why did the tap keep the family awake?
jokes.a: It had a lot to drip about!

maths.problem: In the listening minute, Kavya, a girl in Class 1, heard 3 sounds made by things and 2 sounds made by animals. How many sounds did she hear in all?
maths.explain: Start at 3 and count on 2 more: 4, 5. So Kavya heard 5 sounds in all.
maths.context: This is about the listening minute, when you sat still and counted sounds on your fingers.
maths.why_maths: Adding the groups together shows how many sounds there are in a room that seemed quiet.

maths.problem: On the Sound Scavenger Hunt, Meera, a girl in Class 1, found these sound sources: a fan, a crow, a mixie, rain, a dog, a scooter and the wind. Sort them into 'from nature' and 'made by people'. Which group has more?
maths.answer: From nature: the crow, the rain, the dog and the wind, so 4. Made by people: the fan, the mixie and the scooter, so 3. Nature has 1 more.
maths.explain: Put each source in its group and count each group. 4 is 1 more than 3.
maths.context: This is about the Sound Scavenger Hunt, where you found sounds from nature and sounds made by people.
maths.why_maths: Sorting into groups and counting them shows at a glance where most of the sounds came from.

maths.problem: Put these sounds in order, from the softest to the loudest: a bus horn, a whisper, people talking.
maths.answer: A whisper, then people talking, then a bus horn.
maths.explain: A whisper is the softest, because only a little air moves. Talking is louder. A bus horn is the loudest of the three.
maths.context: This is about loud and soft sounds.
maths.why_maths: Putting things in order is how we compare more than two of them at once.

maths.problem: In the Body Band, Asha, a girl in Class 1, plays a pattern: clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap, stamp. What sound comes next?
maths.explain: The pattern is clap, clap, stamp, and it starts again. After the second stamp comes a new clap, clap, stamp. So the next sound is a clap.
maths.context: This is about the Body Band, where you made sounds with your hands and feet.
maths.why_maths: Finding the part that repeats lets you say what comes next, which is how music keeps a beat.

warmup.q: What do we call the thing that makes a sound?
Does a still bell make a sound?
warmup.a: No. It rings only when something moves it.

warmup.q: How can you make a clap louder?
Name a sound source that is not alive.
warmup.a: Rain, the wind, a bell or a mixie.

warmup.q: Which made a softer sound: a spoon landing on a pillow or on the floor?

roots.context: We have shaken bottles, dropped spoons and listened with our eyes closed. Now we ask what sounds tell us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your bottle of chana made no sound while it sat still. Shake it, and it rattled at once. Every sound you found came from something moving. So whenever you hear a sound, something somewhere is moving right now.
deep_truth.habit: We talk as if a sound belongs to a thing, as in 'the bell's ring'. Yet a still bell is silent. A sound comes from something happening: a moment when something moves.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Shaker Test, every shaker was silent on the table and rattled only while it was shaken. In the listening minute and in Sound Detective, each sound led back to something moving: a fan, a bird, keys, paper, water.

three.who_am_i: You are a sound source too. When you talk, sing or clap, part of you moves, and other people hear it.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings make sounds to find each other: a calf calling her mother, crows warning their family, crickets chirping at night.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is always moving, so it is full of sounds: wind, rain, waves, birds and traffic. Even a quiet room has a fan or a fridge moving.

roots.thread: Your still hands made no sound, and your moving hands did. The chana, the bell and the crow were the same: each sound came from something moving. Everything that moves is aware in its own way, the chana and the bottle too. Many scientists disagree: they say only beings with nerves are aware.

teachings.source: Hakuin Ekaku, a Zen teacher in Japan (1686 to 1769), who gave this question to his students
teachings.teaching: Two hands clap, and there is a sound. What is the sound of one hand?
teachings.link: In the Body Band, a clap came only when two hands moved and met. Hakuin asked this question to make his students stop and listen deeply. It has no quick answer.

teachings.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika, chapter 4, on listening to nada, the inner sound
teachings.teaching: Sit still and listen closely. The text says the sounds you hear at first are loud, like the sea or drums. As you keep listening, they grow finer, like a flute or a humming bee.
teachings.link: In the listening minute, you heard the loud sounds first. The longer you stayed still, the more soft sounds you noticed.

science.text: Every sound is made by something moving back and forth. When the movement stops, the sound stops.
Many animals make sounds that people rarely notice, like fish drumming underwater.

other_view.view: They say chana, bottles and bells are not aware of anything. To them, a sound is only moving things pushing on the air. They think awareness belongs to living beings with nerves or brains.

practice.title: Still hands, moving hands
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Hold your hands still in your lap. Can you hear them? Now rub your palms together very slowly. Listen. Now rub them fast. Is the sound louder? Now stop, and hold your hands still again. Listen to the quiet. Where did the sound go?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Hold your hands still. Now rub them slowly. Listen. Now rub them fast. Now stop. Listen to the quiet.

ask: Your still hands made no sound, and your rubbing hands did. Was the sound in your hands, or in the rubbing?
If everything in the world stopped moving, what would you hear?
When you hear a crow, you know a crow is there and calling. What else can a sound tell you?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed, palms rubbing together with small sound lines, and the same child with still hands and no lines.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people thought the sea was a silent place, and that fish made no sounds. During the Second World War, sailors in the American navy listened to the sea with underwater microphones. They heard grunts, croaks, drumming and crackling. The noise made it hard to listen for submarines. So the navy asked a scientist, Marie Poland Fish, to find out what was making the noise. She and her team kept fish and other sea animals in tanks, and recorded one kind at a time. Croaker fish drum with special muscles against a bag of gas inside their bodies. Tiny snapping shrimp crackle by snapping one big claw shut so fast that it makes a popping bubble. Marie Poland Fish recorded the sounds of many kinds of sea animals. She showed that the sea is full of sound sources. Many kinds of croaker live along India's coasts too.
how_we_found_out.who: Marie Poland Fish (1900 to 1989), an American scientist who studied sea animals, and her team
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The sea is silent, and fish make no sounds. Recording one kind of sea animal at a time showed that croakers drum and snapping shrimp crackle.

founder: ideas/by_topic/sound.md, 'Sources of sound': the sound scavenger hunt (five natural and five made sources) became the Sound Scavenger Hunt. Guessing hidden sounds and matching sounds to sources became Sound Detective. Body percussion and call-and-response rhythm became My Body Band. The journal of sounds became the sound map and the sound diary in the story. The founder's vibration experiments (rubber-band guitar, rice on a drum, straw reeds) belong to the Level 3 unit, so this unit does not repeat them.

Curriculum entry sci.sound.sources-of-sound.L1 (Where do sounds come from? Loud and soft sounds around us), Cambridge Stage 1 unit 6.1. The Level 3 unit sci.sound.sources-of-sound.L3 teaches vibration, sound waves and the medium, with the ruler, foil-ball and atta-drum experiments, the coin line, Katy Payne and the elephants, and the tree-in-the-forest puzzle. This unit only prepares for those: it says sound comes from something moving, and names 'vibrate' as a word for Class 3.
science: Marie Poland Fish (1900 to 1989) catalogued sounds of fish and other marine animals for the US Office of Naval Research from the 1940s, at the Narragansett Marine Laboratory, University of Rhode Island. Fish, M. P. and Mowbray, W. H., Sounds of Western North Atlantic Fishes (Johns Hopkins Press, 1970).
Croakers and drums (family Sciaenidae) make sound with sonic muscles that vibrate the swim bladder.

Snapping shrimp: the snap makes a cavitation bubble whose collapse makes the sound. Versluis, Schmitz, von der Heydt and Lohse, 'How snapping shrimp snap: through cavitating bubbles', Science 289 (2000).
Field crickets: males chirp by rubbing a file on one forewing against a scraper on the other (stridulation).
The dawn chorus: hypotheses include low light for foraging, better sound transmission at dawn and signalling of fitness. None is fully settled.
The koel's loud 'koo-ooo' call is the male's. The male Asian koel is glossy black with red eyes.

Hakuin Ekaku (1686 to 1769) gave the koan of the sound of one hand. Hatha Yoga Pradipika, chapter 4, describes nadanusandhana: inner sounds heard first like the ocean, clouds and drums, later like the flute, the vina and bees.

playtest: Walked through every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge as a parent and child in a flat, with 2 players and with 4 for the games. The Shaker Test and Soft Landing work with kitchen things, and the shaker fair test says plainly that only what is inside differs; the Shaker Test now ends by asking what the shakers did while still. Sound Detective plays with two, and its card-reading rules now say who reads the card and when the detective turns away. Stamp, Tiptoe, Freeze has an ending and says what happens after a swap. Made-up children are introduced, family members are no longer assumed in steps or pictures, repeated questions were replaced (the stretch spoon-and-pillow question now asks about distance), and weak jokes were cut. The three videos still have no checked address.
